Ontario Premier Doug Ford is over the moon about the idea, though he seems most excited about the prospect of expanding Toronto’s Island Airport — an idea
thwarted, at least for now,
by the Carney Liberals. Carney is “on fire,” Ford declared this week on the PM’s policy cavalcade … on the same day the premier endorsed legendary Island Airport-hating Toronto mayor Olivia Chow for re-election. (His office
later insisted he
hadn’t
endorsed her
. You can listen and decide for yourself.)
Article content
In substance, federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre’s position isn’t as different as you might expect from Lewis’s and Stiles’, considering he’s the fellow who
gave the annual Margaret Thatcher Lecture
in London earlier this year. “Canadians are already cash-strapped and broke. We want to make sure that it doesn’t end up being sweetheart deals for corporate power brokers and Liberal insiders at the expense of hard-working Canadians,” he avers. “We want to see how it’s going to save money for Canadians, because if it doesn’t save money, then why do it?”
Article content
Article content
It’s a wise message politically, considering the country’s populist mood … but then, the Canadian public seems to be willing to follow Carney and his policy team just about anywhere these days. Some of us do pine for some old-fashioned ideology, though.

“State control is fundamentally bad because it denies people the power to choose and the opportunity to bear responsibility for their own actions,”
Thatcher wrote in a 2006 piece
for the libertarian Reason Foundation. “Conversely, privatization shrinks the power of the state and free enterprise enlarges the power of the people.”
Article content
Could this plan wind up enriching “Liberal insiders”? Quite possibly; probably, even. But surely privatizing airport operations — as opposed to selling off the assets, which is not on the table — is
less
an invitation to political meddling than having governments or their arm’s-length “not-for-profit” agencies in charge.
Article content
This debate is a classic Canadian confusion between form and function, combined with our crippling suspicion of change — pretty much
any
change. We mustn’t have “privatized” health care … even though we already do, in many respects, and no one really proposes nationalizing pharmacists or blood labs. During the worst days at long-term care homes during the pandemic, the Ontario media fixated on the fact publicly owned facilities seemed to be faring better as a group than privately owned ones. But the vast majority of long-term care homes in Quebec are publicly owned, and they produced similar horrors. The issue is oversight, not ownership.

Several reasonable commentators have suggested it was a misstep for Carney to mention all this right now. It strikes me more like the perfect time.
Article content
Toronto Star columnist Adam Radwanski wondered why the PM would drop such a “contentious type of investment into the mix” at an otherwise-successful investment summit. But surely the whole point of the summit was to attract investment, including foreign investment from (as Radwanski put it) “all the visiting wealth … from Middle Eastern sovereign funds to American private-equity giants.”
Article content
Why would we be concerned about “sovereignty” in one industry and not others? Say what you will about Middle Eastern sovereign funds, they’ve invested in some pretty decent airports — as have Canadian pension plans, in other countries — notably London’s Heathrow. There are terrible airports in Canada under current management (Montreal) and pretty decent ones (Vancouver, which placed 10th in Skytrax’s most recent World Airport awards, higher than any other North American entrant).
Article content
There are crummy and excellent publicly owned airports and crummy and excellent privately owned airports. And we’re not even talking about
ownership
, just management.
Article content
The most frustrating thing is imagining this all coming to naught, for whatever reason, and Canadians just going back to hating the status quo at our biggest airports — Toronto and Montreal, anyway — but never demanding better. It’s one of our natural afflictions.

Opinion: A clarion call for Canadians to stand against Jew hatred The Jewish new year should be a time for Canadians to take stock of the antisemitism happening right under our noses A rabbi blows a shofar in Montreal in 2021.
Photo by Pierre Obendrauf/MONTREAL GAZETTE
Article content
In the Jewish tradition, the 10 days between the celebration of Rosh Hashanah and the observance of Yom Kippur are known as the “Ten Days of Repentance” or the “Days of Awe.” Jewish tradition teaches that the Book of Life is written on Rosh Hashanah, but it is only on Yom Kippur that it is sealed. We are taught that our actions matter and can ultimately alter the decree.

These are difficult, uncertain and painful times. Holocaust survivor and psychiatrist Viktor Frankl taught us that, “Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose our response.”
Article content
For three years, this country’s Jewish community has been hoping that Canadians will stand up and refuse to accept the continued, virulent and persistent vilification of Jews, thinly disguised as anger at the current Israeli government or anti-Zionism. Canadians have a choice to make.
Article content
Too often, it is only when Jews are targeted that people have the audacity to explain away hatred. Why is it that anti-Zionism is tolerated when Zionism — the Jewish right to self-determination in our ancestral homeland — forms the core identity of the vast majority of Jews?
Article content
Would any other religion, race or ethnic group be subject to questions about their lived experiences and what hate feels like to them? A foundational principal in anti-racism work is: nothing about us without us. Except when it comes to the Jews, apparently.
Article content
Article content
When political rhetoric becomes a vehicle for denying Jews the right to national self-determination, when Jewish students are targeted because of their connection to Israel or when tropes about Jewish power, conspiracy and collective guilt are repackaged as political activism, Canadians should have the courage to call it what it is: Jew hatred.

Two recent reports should serve as a wake-up call. Judge Mary Lou Benotto’s independent review at Toronto Metropolitan University examined serious incidents surrounding campus protests and concluded that the events were problematic and symptomatic of a deteriorating campus climate that requires remediation.
Article content
The federal government’s Campus Antisemitism and Student Experiences
report’s
findings are also deeply disturbing, with 84 per cent of Jewish respondents saying antisemitism is a serious problem on campus and more than 95 per cent saying they experienced or witnessed at least one instance of antisemitism in the previous year.
Article content
And our universities are but a microcosm of trends within the broader Canadian society. In July, Statistics Canada data showed that Jews continued to be the most targeted religious group in the country in 2025, accounting for 71 per cent of all religion-motivated hate crimes, despite comprising less than one per cent of the population.

Even more concerning is that political leaders no longer universally condemn Jew hatred. When Edmonton Coun.
Michael Janz wrote
horrible and malicious lies about Israel, Mayor Andrew Knack failed to condemn him, instead saying: “Well, I would say anyone that’s not sharing accurate information, that’s not what we want to see.” His lack of condemnation is a green light for haters to declare open season on Canadian Jews.
Article content
Many years ago, human rights activist Natan Sharansky identified the three Ds of antisemitism — double standards, delegitimization and demonization — that help us understand Jew hatred pertaining to Israel.
Article content
It is a double standard when Israel’s conduct is singled out and not similarly condemned when practised by other democratic countries. Delegitimization is when Israel’s very existence is portrayed as illegitimate or Jews are denied the right to self-determination. Demonization is when Israel or Jews are portrayed using extreme, dehumanizing or conspiratorial language or imagery.
Article content
An example of how the three Ds manifest themselves can be seen at the United Nations. According to data from UN Watch, between 2015 and 2024, the UN General Assembly passed 173 resolutions against Israel, compared with 80 concerning all other countries combined.
Article content
Article content
While the UN has a long history of singling out Israel, these types of double standards have now migrated to Canada. It’s why, across the country, security was particularly robust at all Jewish institutions on Rosh Hashanah, and why rabbis devoted entire sermons to the topic of antisemitism.
Article content
It is hard to say what the tipping point will be as to when Canadian Jews will start looking for safer places to live. As leaders of the National Holocaust Monument Committee, we think about this a lot, but have not yet lost hope that the pendulum can swing and Canada can once again be a safe country for Jews to live in.
Article content
To bring us back to Victor Frankl, we choose to hope that you — our fellow Canadians — will stand up to Jew hatred. We choose to believe that you can influence political leaders and university administrations to take meaningful action against antisemitism.
Article content
At the conclusion of Yom Kippur, the shofar, akin to a trumpet, is blown. I urge all Canadians to hear it as a clarion call to action. Hear it as an urgent appeal to confront Jew hatred.
Article content
Jewish tradition teaches that, “It is not your responsibility to finish the work, but neither are you free to desist from it.” There is no singular way to combat the scourge of antisemitism, but Canada’s Jews need more from our fellow citizens. We need more people speaking out when they see the 3Ds actualized, in whatever form.
Article content
May the blast of the shofar be a wake up call for us all.
Article content
Hear the shofar, and act, before it’s too late.
